Today We Try: Making Pizza in the Middle of a Farm in Hong Kong at @newzealand_organicfarm_hk 🇭🇰🍕👩🏽‍🌾🌾 

📍New Zealand Organic Farm @newzealand_organicfarm_hk 

This is by far one of my favourite experiences in Hong Kong! The family run farm is so cute, and they provide all the essentials for making your own pizza (just bring your own meat & drinks) 👩🏽‍🌾 

The best part? You get to pick your own veggies fresh from their HUGE farm! 🌽🌶️🍃 We had the freshest basil, sweet corn, spicy chillies, and so much more. Everything tastes even better when you’ve picked it yourself! 

It’s such a fun activity whether you’re going as a couple, with friends, or even a big groups! Also perfect for birthday parties and special occasions! It’s so peaceful, surrounded by nature, and just good times all around. 🌾 

It’s a 10/10 for me and something you HAVE to try. Perfect for an escape from the city! Don’t miss out! 🇭🇰

Custom Mahjong Tiles in Hong Kong? 🇭🇰🀄️😱

📍Chi Ming Mahjong, 60 Fa Yuen Street, Mong Kok

This local family run business in Mong Kok creates custom mahjong tiles all carved by hand that are truly one of a kind. It takes 3 days to make, and you can personalize it to make your tiles a perfect reflection of your style. 🤩 

But that’s not all—they also have so many other game aets such as poker and tai sai making it a paradise for game lovers and collectors alike! Whether you’re a Mahjong enthusiast or looking for a unique gift, this shop is a must-visit. 🀄

@hotelkomugiskytree A modern Japanese whole-house stay in Sumida, with a maple view, warm wood, and room to settle in across three floors 🍁

There is history in Hotel Komugi Skytree, but the stay feels bright, calm, and made for the way people travel now. Start with tea in the kitchen, wander out for neighborhood restaurants and Asakusa, then come back to a private house where everyone can stay.

Four bedrooms, nine beds, two bathrooms, a full kitchen, and in-unit laundry make longer Tokyo days easier. Oshiage Station is a three-minute walk away, with direct train connections to both Narita and Haneda; guests also mention the nearby shops, generous space, beautiful interiors, and thoughtful, responsive hosting.

5.0 average on Airbnb across 23 reviews, with top scores for accuracy, cleanliness, and communication. One guest called it the best Airbnb of their Japan trip; others loved being able to walk easily to trains, food, and everyday essentials.

Before you book:
- The bedrooms and shared spaces are spread across three floors, with stairs only
- The house is on a main road, so lighter sleepers may prefer the rooms at the far end
- Check-in is fully self-service, and the whole house is private for your reservation

Poché - Studio Gang | episode 2 of 3

Completed in May 2023, Studio Gang’s Richard Gilder Center for Science, Education, and Innovation is a 230,000-square-foot addition to New York’s American Museum of Natural History. Studio Gang approached the building as an act of architectural grafting: rather than creating an isolated object, the addition stitches together a museum campus that had accumulated over 150 years. It creates 33 connections to 10 existing buildings, replacing dead ends with continuous circulation.

The design is conceived as a geological landscape shaped by wind, water, erosion, and flow. Its five-story Griffin Atrium forms the heart of the building, resembling a canyon whose irregular walls, bridges, stairs, and openings encourage exploration. The architecture was conceived from the inside out, with circulation and visual connections determining the building’s form.

Its most significant innovation is structural. The canyon-like walls are load-bearing shotcrete, sprayed directly onto digitally modeled and custom-bent rebar without conventional formwork. This allowed Studio Gang and engineers Arup to achieve the non-repetitive curves economically while reducing construction waste. The technique was particularly appropriate to the museum because shotcrete was originally developed by museum naturalist Carl Akeley. Extensive mock-ups and digital modeling were required to resolve the complex geometry and construction process.

Externally, the building uses Milford pink granite, echoing the museum’s historic Central Park West entrance, while its masonry courses reference Manhattan schist. This gives the contemporary addition a material relationship to its historic neighbors.

The major challenge was therefore not simply creating an expressive form, but integrating structure, circulation, historic fabric, construction technology, and landscape into one coherent intervention. The result is a building where the architecture itself becomes part of the museum’s lesson about natural processes, scientific discovery, and exploration.

~poché: the space between
